content: The process of updating systematic reviews related to maternal health clinical guidance was conducted following Cochrane's standard procedures. When no suitable systematic reviews (Cochrane or non-Cochrane) were available for priority questions, the World Health Organization (WHO) commissioned new systematic reviews of quantitative studies from external experts. Additional systematic reviews were also carried out to address priority questions and other WHO recommendations on maternal and newborn care, focusing on achieving a positive postnatal experience. These reviews considered both quantitative and qualitative evidence within the Grading of Recommendations Assessment, Development, and Evaluation (GRADE) evidence-to-decision (EtD) frameworks. The WHO Steering Group collaborated closely with members of the Technical Working Group (TWG) to develop or update review protocols, evaluate evidence, and prepare the GRADE EtD frameworks. Representatives from organizations such as the Bill & Melinda Gates Foundation, the International Federation of Gynecology and Obstetrics (FIGO), the International Confederation of Midwives (ICM), the International Pediatric Association (IPA), UNICEF, UNFPA, and USAID were invited to participate in guideline development meetings as observers. These organizations, which have a history of collaboration with WHO, are potential implementers of the guidelines. Observers were allowed to provide comments during technical discussions but were excluded from discussions on final recommendations. The WHO Steering Group, in consultation with systematic review teams, guideline methodologists, and selected members of the Guideline Development Group (GDG), drafted priority questions for the guideline. Changes to the approved scope of the guideline and their justifications are detailed in supplementary materials. The guideline's focus was on essential, routine postnatal care interventions already covered in existing WHO guidelines. The scoping process emphasized identifying person-centered interventions and outcomes for postnatal care. A qualitative evidence synthesis was conducted to understand women's needs, preferences, and values during the postnatal period. This review highlighted that the postnatal phase is a time of significant transition, marked by changes in self-identity, redefined relationships, personal growth opportunities, and adjustments to sexual behavior. Many women also experience intense joy and love for their newborns during this period. Outcomes critical to women and newborns during the postnatal period were prioritized based on the findings of the prioritization exercise. Due to variations in the types of prioritized interventions and their potential outcomes, outcomes were prioritized separately for individual guideline questions. A positive postnatal experience was defined as one where women, partners, caregivers, and families receive consistent information and reassurance from motivated health workers. The health, social, and developmental needs of both women and babies are recognized within a well-resourced and culturally respectful health system. To harmonize and consolidate recommendations relevant to the care of healthy women and newborns during the postnatal period, existing WHO recommendations were integrated into this guideline. Most recommendations were adopted without modification, as they were considered current. Some recommendations required adaptation, which was confirmed feasible by the relevant WHO departments. Integrated recommendations are clearly indicated in the guideline text. The guideline's focus was on essential postnatal care for all women, adolescents, and their newborns to facilitate a positive postnatal experience. The GRADE EtD framework was used to synthesize and evaluate evidence across domains such as benefits, harms, values, resources, equity, acceptability, and feasibility. WHO workstreams included systematic reviews of effectiveness, qualitative evidence synthesis, and assessments of equity and cost-effectiveness. Evidence on maternal clinical practices was primarily derived from Cochrane systematic reviews of randomized controlled trials (RCTs). Where Cochrane reviews were outdated, authors were invited to update them. New systematic reviews were commissioned with clear protocols, including population, intervention, comparator, and outcome (PICO) questions. Qualitative reviews were also commissioned to explore women's preferences for postnatal care, their experiences, and the perspectives of health workers and caregivers. These reviews used validated appraisal tools to assess study quality. The GRADE approach was applied to appraise the certainty of quantitative evidence, with outcomes rated as high, moderate, low, or very low certainty. Qualitative evidence was assessed using the GRADE-CERQual tool, which evaluates confidence in evidence from qualitative research. The WHO Steering Group supervised the preparation of evidence profiles and summaries using the GRADE DECIDE EtD framework. This tool systematically considers evidence on prioritized interventions across specified domains. Recommendations were categorized as recommended, not recommended, recommended only in specific contexts, recommended only in the context of rigorous research, or recommended with targeted monitoring and evaluation. Integrated recommendations were also classified according to this typology. During GDG meetings, members reviewed evidence summaries and EtD frameworks to reach consensus on each recommendation's direction and context. The GDG identified research gaps, particularly where evidence certainty was low or very low, and prioritized further research to address these gaps. The guideline also considered health equity, emphasizing interventions that reduce health inequalities among women and families.
